questions.q: What are Kimball's four dimensional design steps, in the correct order?
options: Identify the facts, identify the dimensions, declare the grain, choose the business process
Identify the dimensions, identify the facts, choose the business process, declare the grain
Choose the business process, declare the grain, identify the dimensions, identify the facts
Declare the grain, choose the business process, identify the facts, identify the dimensions
questions.explain: Each step depends on the one before it: the business process has to be chosen before grain can be declared, and grain has to be locked before dimensions or facts can be correctly identified.

questions.q: What is a "business process," precisely, in this method?
options: A synonym for a dimension table
A department in the org chart, like "Sales" or "Shipping"
Any table that already exists in the OLTP source system
An organizational activity to measure, tied to an identifiable operational event — not a department or existing report
questions.explain: "Sales" alone is too vague — "order processing" and "shipping" are two distinct business processes, each tied to its own operational event and deserving its own fact table.

questions.q: Why is choosing the wrong business process the most expensive mistake in the method?
options: Every later step (grain, dimensions, facts) inherits the mistake, so fixing it usually means rebuilding the fact table from scratch
It only affects the table's column names, which are easy to rename
Business process choice can always be changed after the warehouse is in production with no rework
It has no real consequence as long as the grain is declared correctly
questions.explain: Because steps 2-4 all depend on step 1, getting the business process wrong means every subsequent design decision was made against the wrong foundation.

questions.q: Why must the grain be declared before dimensions and facts are identified?
options: SQL Server enforces this order automatically when creating tables
Because whether a given dimension or measure column belongs in the table depends entirely on what the row's grain is
Dimensions must always be identified before any other step, regardless of grain
Grain has no bearing on which dimensions or facts are valid
questions.explain: A column like ProductKey only belongs at an order-line grain, not an order-level grain — you can't correctly choose dimensions or facts without first knowing the grain they need to fit.

questions.q: What real-world symptom shows up when the four steps are done out of order (e.g. dimensions chosen before grain is locked)?
options: The dimension tables become fact tables instead
The warehouse automatically rejects the table creation
The fact table ends up needing "and"/"or" in its grain statement — the mixed-grain problem from the previous lesson
Nothing — order has no effect on the resulting design
questions.explain: Skipping ahead in the sequence is exactly how a table ends up mixing two grains under one roof, which breaks additive summarization across the table's rows.
